group.title: Environment and sustainability
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To use up a supply of something so that little or none is left.
examples: Intensive farming has {depleted} the soil of nutrients.
wrong: The heavy rain depleted the lake, filling it to the top.

words.meaning: Having a limit; existing only in a fixed amount.
examples: Oil is a {finite} resource that will eventually run out.
wrong: Sunlight is finite, so it will run out next year.

words.meaning: To balance the effect of something by doing something that has the opposite effect.
examples: The airline lets passengers {offset} their emissions by funding tree planting.
wrong: He offset his flight’s emissions by taking three more flights.

words.meaning: Adding no extra carbon dioxide to the air overall, by cutting or balancing emissions.
examples: The company aims to be {carbon neutral} by 2035.
wrong: The factory became carbon neutral by burning twice as much coal.

words.meaning: Able to break down naturally in the environment without causing harm.
examples: These cups are {biodegradable} and rot away in a few months.
wrong: Biodegradable plastic stays in the ground unchanged for centuries.

words.meaning: A mix of rotted plants and food waste used to make soil richer.
examples: We turn our vegetable peelings into {compost} for the garden.
wrong: Compost is a chemical spray that kills every plant it touches.

words.meaning: To make something dirty or harmful by adding a dangerous substance.
examples: Waste from the mine {contaminated} the river.
wrong: The filter contaminated the water, making it perfectly clean.

words.meaning: Getting gas or oil out of rock by forcing liquid into the ground at high pressure.
examples: Residents protested against {fracking} near their village.
wrong: Fracking is a way to collect rainwater from rooftops.

words.meaning: The process of fertile land slowly turning into desert.
examples: Overgrazing has sped up {desertification} in the region.
wrong: Thanks to desertification, the dry land became green and fertile.

words.meaning: The slow wearing away of land or rock by wind, water or ice.
examples: Tree roots help prevent soil {erosion} on hillsides.
wrong: Erosion built the cliff higher every year.

words.meaning: A state where the greenhouse gases a country or company adds are balanced by those it removes.
examples: The government has promised to reach {net zero} by 2050.
wrong: Reaching net zero means doubling the gases you release.

words.meaning: A system where products are reused, repaired and recycled instead of thrown away.
examples: In a {circular economy}, old phones become parts for new ones.
wrong: The circular economy depends on throwing products away after one use.

words.meaning: Connected with the relationship between living things and their environment.
examples: The oil spill was an {ecological} disaster for the coast.
wrong: The ecological damage only affected the company’s bank account.

words.meaning: A person who works to protect the natural world.
examples: {Environmentalists} campaigned to save the ancient forest.
wrong: The environmentalist led a campaign to cut down the forest for profit.

words.meaning: Using more goods or resources than is needed or than nature can replace.
examples: {Overconsumption} in rich countries puts heavy pressure on the planet.
wrong: Overconsumption means buying only the few things you truly need.

words.meaning: To protect something or use it carefully so it is not wasted or destroyed.
examples: Turn off the tap while brushing to {conserve} water.
wrong: They conserved energy by leaving every light on all night.

words.meaning: To damage something so that its quality or condition becomes worse.
examples: Plastic waste {degrades} marine habitats.
wrong: The cleanup degraded the beach, leaving it spotless.

words.meaning: Planting trees again in an area where a forest was cut down or destroyed.
examples: The {reforestation} project has planted a million trees.
wrong: Reforestation means clearing the last trees from a hillside.

words.meaning: Technology that collects carbon dioxide from factories or the air and stores it underground.
examples: The power plant is testing {carbon capture} to cut its emissions.
wrong: Carbon capture releases extra carbon dioxide into the sky.

words.meaning: To make a company or product seem better for the environment than it really is.
examples: The brand was accused of {greenwashing} its plastic bottles with leafy labels.
wrong: The firm greenwashed its products by honestly listing all their harmful effects.

words.meaning: Not harmful to the environment.
examples: They switched to {eco-friendly} cleaning products.
wrong: The eco-friendly detergent poisoned the fish in the stream.

words.meaning: Catching so many fish that their numbers cannot recover.
examples: {Overfishing} has caused cod stocks to collapse.
wrong: Overfishing allowed the fish population to grow quickly.

words.meaning: The careful and responsible management of something, such as land or resources.
examples: Farmers practice good {stewardship} by protecting the soil for future generations.
wrong: Their stewardship of the park left it ruined and full of litter.

words.meaning: A situation where there is not enough of something.
examples: Water {scarcity} is a growing problem in dry regions.
wrong: Because of scarcity, there was more water than anyone could use.

words.meaning: To send out gas, heat, light or sound into the air.
examples: Older cars {emit} more harmful gases.
wrong: Solar panels emit thick black smoke when the sun shines.

words.meaning: Energy from sources that do not run out, such as wind, sun and water.
examples: The country now gets half its electricity from {renewables}.
wrong: Coal and oil are the most common renewables.

words.meaning: Made to be used once and then thrown away.
examples: The city has banned {single-use} plastic bags.
wrong: Her single-use water bottle has lasted ten years of daily refills.

words.meaning: Dangerous, especially to health or the environment.
examples: {Hazardous} chemicals must be disposed of at special sites.
wrong: The hazardous waste was safe enough to drink.

words.meaning: Rainwater that flows off land into rivers, often carrying soil or chemicals.
examples: Fertilizer {runoff} from farms is turning the lake green.
wrong: Runoff is water that stays still in the soil and never moves.

words.meaning: The average height of the surface of the sea, used to measure land height.
examples: Melting ice is causing {sea levels} to rise.
wrong: The village is so far below sea level that it sits on a mountain top.

words.meaning: A thick layer of ice that permanently covers a large area of land, especially near the poles.
examples: Scientists measure how fast the polar {ice caps} are shrinking.
wrong: The ice cap melted completely during one cold winter night.

words.meaning: A charge that companies or people pay based on how much carbon dioxide they produce.
examples: A {carbon tax} makes polluting fuels more expensive.
wrong: The carbon tax rewards factories for burning more coal.

words.meaning: To fill something up again after it has been used.
examples: Heavy rains finally {replenished} the reservoir.
wrong: The drought replenished the lake to its highest level.

words.meaning: Illegally hunting or catching wild animals.
examples: {Poaching} has driven rhinos close to extinction.
wrong: Poaching means caring for wild animals in a legal sanctuary.

words.meaning: To reuse an old item to make something of better quality or value.
examples: She {upcycled} old jeans into a stylish bag.
wrong: He upcycled the chair by throwing it in the trash.

words.meaning: The distance produce travels from the farm where it is grown to your plate.
examples: Buying local produce cuts down your {food miles}.
wrong: Food miles measure how many calories a meal contains.

words.meaning: A band of gas high above the earth that protects us from the sun’s harmful rays.
examples: Some old chemicals put holes in the {ozone layer}.
wrong: The ozone layer is a layer of rock deep under the ocean floor.

words.meaning: Precipitation made harmful by polluting gases in the air, which damages trees, lakes and buildings.
examples: {Acid rain} has eaten away at the old stone statues.
wrong: Acid rain is clean water that helps forests grow.

words.meaning: Fuel made from plants or organic waste instead of oil or coal.
examples: Some buses now run on {biofuel} made from used cooking oil.
wrong: Biofuel is made by digging up coal from deep mines.

words.meaning: Growing only one type of crop over a large area, year after year.
examples: Vast {monocultures} of palm oil have replaced rainforest.
wrong: The farm was a monoculture, with dozens of different crops in each field.
